VBO:0200651.summary: Halden Hounds tend to be friendly, trusting and open with people, while retaining a strong appetite for the hare trail. Breeders near Halden shaped the hound from local dogs and imported foxhounds and beagles in the late 1800s; enthusiasts rebuilt the line after disease and World War II nearly ended it.
VBO:0200651.shortDescription: Friendly and trusting off the trail, this Norwegian hound comes alive on a hare trail.
VBO:0200651.historicalRoots: Norwegian hare-hound developed around Halden in the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: Norwegian Kennel Club: Haldenstøver
sources.evidence: NKK Haldenstøver page supports friendly, trusting and sociable character plus hare-hunting drive; records late-1800s crosses of local hounds with English foxhounds and beagles, 1931 canine plague and World War II decline, and postwar rebuilding.

VBO:0200588.summary: German Giant Spitz dogs are lively, attentive and strongly attached to their people. Their teachability and natural reserve with strangers suit a home-and-farm watchdog role, while the breed standard describes little hunting instinct. The same standard also prizes their weather hardiness and robust constitution.
VBO:0200588.shortDescription: Lively and attentive, the white Giant Spitz shares a German home-and-farm watchdog heritage.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 97 — German Spitz (Giant section)
sources.evidence: FCI 97 Giant/Medium/Miniature section pp. 8–9 states attentive, lively, attached, teachable character, stranger reserve, lack of hunting instinct, home-and-farm watch role, weather indifference and robustness; pp. 12–13 define Giant size and white coat.

VBO:0201149.summary: Russian Hounds tend to be calm and balanced between hunts, yet are valued for endurance once on a trail. Traditionally they followed hare or fox alone, in a pair or with a pack; hunters prized their far-carrying, musical voice, which shifts tone as the chase unfolds.
VBO:0201149.shortDescription: Calm off the trail and enduring on it, the Russian Hound has a far-carrying musical hunting voice.
VBO:0201149.historicalRoots: Long Russian scent-hound tradition for hare, fox and other game.

sources.title: Russian Cynological Federation: Russian Hound standard
sources.evidence: RKF behavior gives calm, balanced temperament. Utilization says hunting singly, in a pair or pack on hare, fox and other game. History emphasizes stamina and a strong far-carrying musical voice that changes notes during chase.

VBO:0201010.summary: Petit Bleu de Gascogne hounds are calm and affectionate, yet intent when working a scent. They cooperate well in a pack and are known for a fine nose and a beautiful voice; hare is a favored quarry, though the standard also records big-game work. The breed came from a deliberate reduction in size of the Grand Bleu de Gascogne, shaped by hunting needs in France.
VBO:0201010.shortDescription: Calm and affectionate, this French pack hound follows hare with a fine nose and distinctive voice.
VBO:0201010.historicalRoots: French Gascony scent hound selected in a smaller size

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 31 — Petit Bleu de Gascogne
sources.evidence: FCI31 pp. 2–4: calm, affectionate, fine nose, voice and pack work; hare favored, big game possible; deliberate reduction from Grand Bleu de Gascogne; French origin; medium hound morphology, dense slate-blue mottling, curled-in ears and hock-length sabre tail.

VBO:0200687.summary: Hygenhounds are friendly, willing hare hunters that are often calm in the house. Their varied calls tell a hunter how far they are from the quarry, making their voice part of the work rather than a background trait. The breed takes its name from Hans Fredrik Hygen, who bred local hounds in Norway from the 1830s.
VBO:0200687.shortDescription: Calm indoors but eager on a hare trail, this Norwegian hound signals distance with its voice.
VBO:0200687.historicalRoots: Norwegian hare-hound developed from local lines by Hans Fredrik Hygen from the 1830s.

sources.title: Norwegian Kennel Club: Hygenhund
sources.evidence: NKK Hygenhund page describes friendly, trainable, work-willing hare hound, calm family behavior, distinct vocal signals of distance to quarry, and Hans Fredrik Hygen breeding local hounds around Ringerike beginning in the 1830s.

VBO:0201188.summary: Standard Schnauzers are playful, alert and devoted, yet the breed standard also describes a composed side. In southern Germany they worked around stables, where their quick response to rodents earned them the name “Rattler.” Keen senses and trainability later supported their place as watch and companion dogs.
VBO:0201188.shortDescription: Playful, alert and devoted, this German stable dog once earned the nickname “Rattler.”
VBO:0201188.historicalRoots: Southern German stable dog and ratter

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 182 — Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI 182 pp. 2–3 describes lively yet placid, playful, devoted, alert temperament; Southern German stable work and rodent nickname Rattler; pp. 4–5 black coat, natural drop ears and tail.

VBO:0201168.summary: Saint-Usuge Spaniels are gentle and affectionate dogs that tend to stay close to their people. In the Bresse woodlands and marshes, they search close to a handler and may retrace their steps to check a scent; they are especially associated with woodcock.
VBO:0201168.shortDescription: Gentle and close-working, this Bresse pointing spaniel checks scent carefully in woodcock country.
VBO:0201168.historicalRoots: Bresse woodland-and-marsh pointing spaniel preserved after World War II by Abbé Robert Billard.

sources.title: Société Centrale Canine: annotated Saint-Usuge Spaniel standard
sources.evidence: Character/function section describes notably gentle and affectionate, close to owners; short-ranging continental pointing search maintaining handler contact, retracing steps to verify scent, specialization in woodcock. Historical section places breed in Bresse forest/marsh and recounts recovery by Abbé Robert Billard.

VBO:0201172.summary: Fringed Salukis pair a dignified, independent manner with a long history of coursing across the Middle East. In Arab tradition they were valued rather than traded, and a Saluki presented to someone was a mark of honour. Dogs from many regions and terrains reached Europe this way; the first British standard in 1923 was written broadly enough to embrace those varied types.
VBO:0201172.shortDescription: Dignified and independent, this fringed Saluki carries a long coursing history and silky feathering.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 269 — Saluki
sources.evidence: FCI 269 pp. 2–3 supports dignity, independence, Middle Eastern coursing, honour-gift tradition and broad 1923 British standard covering regional types; pp. 3–4 define silky feathering of fringed coat.

VBO:0200652.summary: The Hällefors Elkhound is an energetic, courageous hunting spitz with endurance for demanding forest work. It is noted for strong elk-hunting instinct and a close bond with one handler. Developed from Hällefors-area dogs in Sweden, this distinct Nordic breed gained Swedish Kennel Club recognition in 2000.
VBO:0200652.shortDescription: Courageous and enduring in elk country, this Swedish spitz bonds closely with one handler.
VBO:0200652.historicalRoots: Swedish elk-hunting spitz shaped from Hällefors-area stock and recognized in 2000.

sources.title: Swedish Kennel Club: Hälleforshund
sources.evidence: SKK Hälleforshund breed page supports high energy, courage, hardy strength, elk-hunting drive, marked one-handler attachment, Hällefors-region origins and recognition in 2000; coat, dark muzzle and high loosely curved tail support morphology.

VBO:0201322.summary: Schwyz Hounds share the Swiss Hound's lively interest in scent, sensitivity and attachment to their handlers. They hunt independently and give voice while searching difficult terrain. White with orange patches or an orange saddle, the Schwyz is one of four varieties brought under a single Swiss Hound standard in 1933.
VBO:0201322.shortDescription: Lively on scent yet sensitive with its handler, this orange-and-white Swiss hound hunts independently.
VBO:0201322.historicalRoots: Orange-and-white Schwyz variety of the Swiss Hound, unified under one standard in 1933.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 59: Swiss Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 059 describes Swiss Hounds as lively, scent-keen, sensitive, docile and attached to the handler, hunting independently with voice on difficult terrain; lists Schwyz as white with orange patches/saddle and records four-variety unified standard in 1933. No coat-specific temperament claim.

VBO:0201317.summary: Swedish White Elkhounds give a calm but alert impression, with energy and endurance behind a strong hunting drive. This Swedish hunting spitz developed from the gray Norwegian Elkhound and Jämthund lines, then gained Swedish Kennel Club recognition in 1993 as a distinct breed.
VBO:0201317.shortDescription: Calm-looking yet alert and energetic, this Swedish hunting spitz has a strong drive for game.
VBO:0201317.historicalRoots: Swedish hunting spitz derived from gray Norwegian Elkhound and Jämthund lines; recognized in 1993.

sources.title: Swedish Kennel Club: Svensk vit älghund
sources.evidence: SKK character section says calm but alert impression, energetic, enduring and strong hunting interest; history says branch of Norwegian gray Elkhound and Jämthund, formally recognized by SKK in 1993.

VBO:0201319.summary: Bernese Hounds are lively and passionately keen on hunting, yet sensitive and strongly attached to their handler. They follow hare, fox or roe deer independently while giving voice, and they search difficult ground with determination.
VBO:0201319.shortDescription: Lively and attached to its handler, this Bernese Hound follows scent independently and gives voice.
VBO:0201319.historicalRoots: Bernese variety of the Swiss Hound, with deep Swiss hunting roots.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 59: Swiss Hound, Bernese variety
sources.evidence: FCI temperament describes lively, passionately keen hunter, sensitive, docile and attached to owner. Utilization states independent voiced hunting on hare, roe deer, fox and sometimes boar with determined searching on difficult ground. FCI lists Bernese as one of four Swiss Hound varieties.

VBO:0201156.summary: Ryukyu dogs can be quiet and responsive with their own people while remaining territorial, agile and keen on scent. Native to Okinawa, they were the focus of a preservation society founded by Yoshio Arakaki, who worked to sustain this distinct island breed.
VBO:0201156.shortDescription: Quiet with its own people but territorial and agile, this Okinawan dog is keen on scent.
VBO:0201156.historicalRoots: Native Okinawan dog preserved through the Ryukyu Dog Preservation Society.

sources.title: Miyako Association bulletin: interview with Ryukyu Dog Preservation Society founder Yoshio Arakaki
sources.evidence: Founder interview describes Ryukyu dogs as quiet and obedient with owners, territorial, agile and strong in scenting; discusses the preservation society and Okinawan native identity.

VBO:0201320.summary: The Jura Hound is a keen, determined scent worker that can follow a trail independently and give voice as it goes. Like the other Swiss Hounds, it is also sensitive, docile and closely attached to its handler. Its tan-and-black coat marks the Jura variety of a breed long prized for hunting hare across difficult ground.
VBO:0201320.shortDescription: Determined on difficult scent trails, this tan-and-black Swiss hound keeps a close handler bond.
VBO:0201320.historicalRoots: Tan-and-black Jura variety of the Swiss Hound, used for hare and other quarry.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 59: Swiss Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 059 supports independent, vocal, determined scent hunting on difficult terrain and breed-wide sensitive/docile/handler-attached character; recognizes the Jura tan-with-black-blanket variety. No variety-specific temperament claim.

VBO:0201148.summary: Russian Harlequin Hounds have a balanced working temperament and were developed for hunts that used coordinated packs. Breeders combined Russian hounds with English foxhound blood, seeking endurance, a keen nose and the strong musical voice needed to follow game through forest.
VBO:0201148.shortDescription: Balanced in temperament, this Russian pack hound was bred for endurance, scent and a musical voice.
VBO:0201148.historicalRoots: Russian Pied/Anglo-Russian hound developed through Russian hound and English foxhound crosses.

sources.title: Russian Cynological Federation: Russian Pied Hound standard
sources.evidence: RKF behavior says balanced. Use/history describes pack work and crossing Russian hounds with imported English foxhounds to combine stamina, scent and strong musical voice; current breed name Russian Pied Hound.

sources.title: Magyar Nyelvőr 2017 breed-nomenclature study
sources.evidence: Linguistic source equates Russian Harlequin, Russian Piebald/Pied and Anglo-Russian hound names with Finnish englantilais-venäläinen ajokoira, establishing exact selected VBO alias for the Commons original.

VBO:0201321.summary: Lucerne Hounds are lively and passionate about following scent, but sensitive and attached to their handlers. They can search independently with voice over difficult ground for hare and other quarry. Their blue-speckled coat with black patches and tan points sets this Swiss Hound variety apart within the shared working breed.
VBO:0201321.shortDescription: Lively and handler-attached, this blue-speckled Swiss hound follows difficult trails with voice.
VBO:0201321.historicalRoots: Blue-speckled Lucerne variety of the Swiss Hound, sharing its independent scent-hunting role.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 59: Swiss Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 059 supports lively, scent-keen, sensitive, docile, handler-attached temperament and independent vocal search on difficult terrain; lists Lucerne blue speckling with black patches/saddle and tan points. No color-specific behavior claim.

VBO:0201403.summary: Weimaraners are steady yet passionate hunting dogs, known for methodical searching and keen scenting. They were kept at the Weimar court by the early 1800s; professional hunters and gamekeepers then shaped the breed across central Germany. The shorthaired variety was established before the rarer longhaired form appeared around the turn of the 20th century.
VBO:0201403.shortDescription: Steady yet keen on a scent, this shorthaired German pointer traces its story to the Weimar court.
VBO:0201403.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and hunting dog

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 99 — Weimaraner
sources.evidence: FCI 99 pp. 2–3 documents steady passionate hunting temperament, scent and systematic search; Weimar court by early 19th century, professional gamekeeper development, short/long coat chronology; pp. 5–6 defines short coat.

VBO:0201108.summary: Pumis are lively, bold herders with an expressive, often vocal way of meeting the world. They developed in Hungary during the 17th and 18th centuries from older Puli stock and imported German and French terrier-type dogs. Herding larger livestock and dealing with rodents are both documented uses; the breed standard also describes a dog restless and ready for action.
VBO:0201108.shortDescription: Lively and bold, this vocal Hungarian herder grew from Puli and terrier-type working stock.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 56 — Pumi
sources.evidence: FCI 56 pp. 2–3 documents lively, bold, expressive and noisy herding character, Hungarian 17th–18th-century Puli/German-French terrier-type origins, livestock/rodent work and restless readiness; p. 6 permits grey.
